sections.content: You know *deber* + infinitive from B1 Unit 4: *Debes descansar* is "You should rest". It names a duty or a piece of advice. Careful Spanish adds a small word to make a different meaning: *deber de* + infinitive is a guess based on evidence. You know *Estará en casa* ("He must be at home") from B1 Unit 22, the future of probability; *Debe de estar en casa* says the same thing. So the rule is: *deber* with no *de* for a duty, *deber de* for a guess.
sections.title: Two small words, two meanings
deber and deber de
rows: Debes llamar a tu abuela hoy.
You should call your grandmother today.
We must all respect the rules.
Las luces están encendidas: debe de estar en casa.
The lights are on: he must be at home.
No contesta el teléfono; debe de haber salido.
He is not answering the phone; he must have gone out.

sections.content: In real life speakers mix the two. You will often hear *Debe estar en casa* for a guess, and some people even say *Debes de llamar* for a duty. Both are understood, but books on grammar call the second one a mistake and prefer to keep *de* for guesses. For your own Spanish, keep the difference: no *de* for a duty, *de* for a guess. For a guess about the past, put *haber* + a past participle after *deber de*: *debe de haber salido*.
